segments: Three Roles: How Secrets Become Process Environment Variables

① sops writes a file: after sops-install-secrets decrypts secrets.yaml, it writes the contents of app_env to /run/secrets/app_env. The usual settings are root:root and 0400; the actual values come from the secret's owner/group/mode. On Linux, sops-nix places secrets in ramfs at /run/secrets.d by default and exposes them through the /run/secrets link. useTmpfs changes the storage mechanism. These are runtime artifacts, regenerated after a reboot.
② systemd injects environment variables (the crucial step):

EnvironmentFile is a systemd feature, not an example-app feature: before starting the service, systemd reads the file and injects KEY=value into the process environment. This happens before the process is created; example-app itself knows nothing about sops.

③ The process consumes them: example-app's ExecStartPre uses envsubst to render config.yaml from environment variables (${APP_SECRET} and ${APP_ENDPOINT}), then ExecStart reads the rendered configuration to start the application.
Decrypted Output: One File per Key

After decryption, sops-nix creates a separate file for each secret; it does not combine them. In the source, the default path is /run/secrets/<secret名> (with neededForUsers, it is /run/secrets-for-users/). Each secret declares its own output path and permissions.
Define three secrets and you get three files:

format can be set per secret (yaml/json/dotenv/ini/binary), but it specifies how to parse the source sopsFile, not the format of an individual value. Secrets from the same YAML source should be read as YAML. For a dotenv or binary source, point to a separate encrypted file in that format. The default format inherits defaultSopsFormat; it is not automatically inferred from the file extension.

Storage Structure vs. Runtime Organization When encrypting, all keys go into one secrets.yaml file (the storage layer). When decrypting, they are split by secret name into multiple separate files (the runtime layer). format selects how the encrypted source is parsed, and key selects the value to export. A YAML string value can itself contain a multiline environment file or configuration text. key = "" exports the entire decrypted file; binary ignores key.
useSystemdActivation: Two Deployment Paths for Regular Secrets
sops-nix can deploy regular secrets through a NixOS activation script or a systemd unit:
Entry Point
setupSecrets during NixOS activation
Execution Conditions
Affected by boot and switch activation, user creation, and mount availability
Ordering is controlled through unit dependencies
Typical Choice
The default depends on the user-management mechanism and module version
Useful when mount dependencies are required or when using sysusers/userborn
What to Check
Whether keys, users, and directories are available at activation time
After, RequiresMountsFor, and dependencies of consuming services

Not all NixOS activation scripts are initrd scripts. Check the boot and activation paths against the configuration version and logs; a missing secret file alone does not identify the stage at which something failed. The current upstream module orders the systemd path against targets such as local-fs.target and sets RequiresMountsFor based on key paths. For an actual deployment, use the code at the project's locked revision and the generated unit as the authority. neededForUsers uses an earlier path, before user creation, and must be checked separately; ordinary service waiting mechanisms cannot fix that path.
Mount Ordering: Why Timing Matters

During decryption, the process running that stage must be able to read the key. Mount availability depends on the boot configuration; it cannot be inferred solely from a directory name or Btrfs subvolume name:
Example Path
Possible Contents
Conditions to Check
Root filesystem and host key
Whether root is persistent and the host key has already been generated or restored
Whether the mounts needed for boot are already available
User identity and configuration
Whether the user partition is mounted and the service has access
Persistent keys and machine state
Mount ordering, restoration bindings, and dependencies of the decryption stage

If the key is on a separate mount point, first check the generated unit and its mount dependencies. Secrets needed before user creation require the restored key to be available at that early stage. Ordinary service secrets can use appropriate systemd mount dependencies. Choose the deployment path first, then decide where to store the key.

Check existence, permissions, and timing first, and avoid printing private keys or decrypted contents. With systemd-based decryption, the consuming service should refer to the actual sops-install-secrets.service and declare appropriate After ordering and dependencies. After only specifies order; it does not start a unit. Requires can express that the consuming service must not start if the decryption service fails.
Why sops-nix Can Reuse an SSH Host Key

When OpenSSH or host-key generation is enabled, the current upstream module imports Ed25519 keys (for age) or RSA keys (for GnuPG) from services.openssh.hostKeys by default, while excluding keys in /run/secrets to avoid circular dependencies. If the relevant functionality is not enabled, the default list can be empty. Not every NixOS machine has a host key.
User id_ed25519
Common Location
/etc/ssh/, which can also be changed through system configuration
The user's ~/.ssh/
Identity
Usually a machine identity managed by root
User identity
Decryption Prerequisites
Generated or restored, with the file and mount available and readable
The user key exists, with suitable permissions and passphrase handling

Reasons to reuse a host key include aligning machine services with the machine identity's lifecycle, reducing the number of independent keys, and readability with root privileges. These are operational choices, not proof that a host key is mandatory or that it will automatically survive a reinstall. Reuse increases the impact of a key leak; a dedicated age key separates SSH identity from the ability to decrypt secrets.
Configuration Example: Move from a Dedicated age Key to a Host Key

The standard host-key paths here are generic examples and contain no actual keys. First add the new recipient to the ciphertext and verify independent decryption, then change the deployment source. Keep the old source until the new path is fully verified. SSH host keys also need a backup and recovery plan; reusing one does not remove the need for migration.

Keys can be stored in a persistent directory suited to the system design, provided it is readable during the relevant decryption stage and dependencies are correct. Do not categorically rule out /persist or /home. Likewise, do not assume /etc is available early simply because it is under the root path.

Service environment variables are a convenient interface, but they are not appropriate for every secret: anyone able to inspect the process environment or the trusted service's execution context may be able to read them. If the application supports credential files, prefer passing a path. Plaintext must not be exposed through Nix evaluation, the store, or build logs.
